findings.title: Redaction bypass: compound env-var names and URL-embedded passwords pass through unchanged
evidence: The key=value pattern uses word-boundary anchors. Python word boundaries sit between \w and \W. Underscore is \w, so in DB_PASSWORD the underscore immediately precedes 'password' — no word boundary exists there. The pattern never fires.
Confirmed live: python3 hooks/lib/redact.py with input {"cmd": "export DB_PASSWORD=hunter2 && run.sh"} returns the string unredacted. Same for DB_SECRET, DB_PASS, APP_SECRET_KEY, MYPASSWORD.

URL-embedded passwords also leak. Input 'psql postgresql://admin:SuperSecret123@db.internal/prod' — password lives between ':' and '@' in RFC-3986 userinfo. No pattern in redact.py covers this syntax. Confirmed live.

GitHub fine-grained PATs (format: github_pat_11XXXX_...) are not matched by the gh[opsu]_ pattern. Confirmed live: github_pat_11ABCDE_longpatternwithlotsofcharsabcdefghijklmnopqrst passes through unchanged.
AWS STS temporary credential keys start with ASIA not AKIA. The AKIA-only pattern misses all temporary STS credentials entirely.

Impact: tool calls that run psql/mysql/redis with a connection URL, export a compound env var, or use a github_pat_ token log the raw secret to ~/.claude/logs/tool-calls-YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl at full fidelity for up to 365 days.

Suggested additions: (1) URL userinfo pattern matching ://[^:@\s]+:([^@\s]{4,})@ ; (2) compound env var pattern without word-boundary requirement, matching [A-Z0-9_]*PASSWORD=[^\s,;'"]{4,} style; (3) github_pat_[A-Za-z0-9_]{30,} ; (4) ASIA[0-9A-Z]{16} for STS keys.

findings.title: Safety-hook bypass: dangerous commands inside quoted strings survive quote-strip and execute unblocked
evidence: safety-block.sh line 16 strips all single-quoted and double-quoted substrings before pattern-matching: S=$(printf '%s' "$CMD" | sed strips double-quoted then single-quoted content).
bash -c 'DANGEROUS_CONTENT_HERE': after stripping single-quoted content becomes 'bash -c '. The string 'rm' is absent from the stripped value. All rm-based patterns miss it. Verified by simulation.
eval "DANGEROUS_CONTENT_HERE": after stripping double-quoted content becomes 'eval '. All patterns that check for the payload keyword miss it.
sh -c 'mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdX': single-quoted payload stripped entirely. mkfs pattern fires on 'mkfs' which is no longer present.

The permissions.deny list in settings.json is a separate upstream gate covering Bash(rm -rf *) and Bash(sudo *). But safety-block.sh owns patterns exclusively not in the deny list, such as the fork-bomb and chmod-777-root patterns. Those can be bypassed by wrapping in bash -c 'FORK_BOMB_HERE'. Confirmed: bash -c ':(){ :|:& };:' strips to 'bash -c ' — fork bomb pattern matches ':()' which is absent.

The comment on line 15 acknowledges this is an approximation. The adversarial finding is that the approximation is systematically exploitable for any command that can be expressed as a string argument to bash/sh/eval/python3 -c.

findings.title: jq hooks merge silently drops user existing hook lists when both settings files share the same event key
evidence: The merge expression: .hooks = ($existing.hooks // {}) * ($new.hooks // {}). jq object multiplication (A * B) for a key present in both A and B where the value is an array: B's array replaces A's array entirely. jq does not concatenate arrays.

Confirmed: jq -s merging existing={hooks:{PreToolUse:[{matcher:Bash,hooks:[{command:user-custom-hook.sh}]}]}} with new={hooks:{PreToolUse:[{command:safety-block.sh}]}} produces output with only safety-block.sh in PreToolUse. user-custom-hook.sh is dropped silently, no warning emitted.
Any user with pre-existing custom PreToolUse or PostToolUse hooks in ~/.claude/settings.json will lose them on first install without any indication.

The idempotency guard (lines 119-125) means that after first install, re-running without --force skips merge entirely. Running with --force re-triggers the same array-overwrite. There is no path that both re-merges and preserves existing user hook lists.
Backup exists (settings.json is copied to BACKUP_DIR), but the merged output silently drops the hooks — user would need to diff the backup to notice the loss.
Fix: replace array-overwriting object multiplication with per-event-key concatenation, e.g. using reduce over event keys to union the arrays, then deduplicate.

findings.title: install.sh: python3 called without availability guard in merge path, leaves settings.json absent on abort
evidence: Failure scenario: jq present, python3 absent (e.g. minimal macOS, or python3 removed after install).
Line 131: backup_existing moves ~/.claude/settings.json to $BACKUP_DIR. settings.json is now absent from its home location.
Lines 135-147: jq runs and writes merged JSON to settings.json.tmp — succeeds.
Line 149: python3 -m json.tool runs as the validation step. python3 not found -> exit 127.
set -euo pipefail (line 2) catches exit 127 and terminates install.sh. Line 151 (mv settings.json.tmp settings.json) never runs.

Result: settings.json is absent (in backup dir), settings.json.tmp has correct merged content but is unrenamed. Claude Code launched afterward starts with no settings.json -> empty defaults: no deny rules, no hooks, no permission configuration.
The python3 availability warning (lines 304-305) appears in the script's post-argument-parse section and fires AFTER install_all() has already been called. The damage precedes the warning.
Fix: add 'command -v python3 >/dev/null 2>&1 ||' guard around line 149, or replace python3 -m json.tool with 'jq . < settings.json.tmp >/dev/null' (jq already confirmed present in this branch).

findings.title: call_id never matches between pre and post log rows — documented pair-join invariant is structurally impossible
evidence: _call_id() returns f'{int(time.time() * 1_000_000)}-{os.getpid()}'. Every invocation returns a different value because time advances and separate processes have distinct PIDs.

Pre-hook (one python3 process): _call_id() is called at line 179 to write to the temp file, and again at line 188 to write to the pre-log payload. These two values are already different within the same pre-hook invocation.
Post-hook (a separate python3 process, different PID, launched later): _call_id() is called at line 245 to write to the post-log payload. Different from both pre-hook values.

The temp file (line 179) stores a call_id value. The post-hook reads it at the split() (lines 200-203) as parts[0]. But parts[0] is never used — only parts[1] (start_time) is consumed. The temp file call_id is discarded.
LOGGING.md states: 'call_id: nanosecond ts + PID; matches pre row to its post row.' This is false. Pre and post row call_ids are always different by construction.

The Slowest tool calls query in LOGGING.md implicitly assumes that pre-row args can be joined to post-row duration by call_id. Since call_ids never match across rows, this cross-row join produces zero results. Duration analytics cannot be correlated with their args.

Fix: in the pre-hook, store the same call_id value in both the temp file and the log payload. In the post-hook, read call_id from the temp file and use it as the post-row's call_id. This requires changing line 179 to write the call_id that will also be used in payload line 188.

findings.title: Concurrent identical tool calls in one session generate the same pair_path, causing post-hook to read wrong start time
evidence: _pair_key(session_id, tool_input) hashes only (session_id, tool_input). Two concurrent calls with identical tool_input in the same session produce an identical pair_path.
Confirmed: pair_key('sess-abc123', {'command': 'git status'}) returns 'sess_abc123-52081f5421982a56' for both concurrent calls — same file path.

CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 is enabled in settings.json env block, enabling multi-agent parallel execution. Multiple parallel agents that each run the same Bash command in the same session will collide on pair_path.

Race sequence: T0 Call-A pre writes start_A to pair_path. T1 Call-B pre overwrites pair_path with start_B. T2 Call-A post reads pair_path, gets start_B -> duration measured from B's start (wrong). T3 Call-B post: pair_path deleted by A. Fallback (lines 210-228) scans for most-recent session-prefixed temp file — may claim a stale file from a different tool call.
Impact: duration_ms is unreliable for any session that runs identical tool calls concurrently. Affects the core logging value proposition for agent-loop sessions where AGENT_TEAMS is active.

findings.title: Unbounded log growth during long sessions: SessionEnd-only rotation cannot fire mid-session; gzip peaks at 2x log size
evidence: log-rotate.sh fires only on SessionEnd. A long-running agent loop accumulates log entries throughout the session with no mid-session rotation trigger.

At 10,000 tool calls in a session with average 500 bytes per entry: ~5 MB typical. At the 1 MB per-line cap with large tool output: up to 9.8 GB before SessionEnd fires. No size-based mid-session rotation exists.

During gzip rotation (line 30): gzip -c writes the compressed file while the original remains. A 100 MB log compressing to 20 MB creates 120 MB peak usage. If free space is between 100 MB and 120 MB, gzip fails mid-write. The && operator prevents rm from running (original preserved), but the partial .gz file is left on disk at .N.gz.

On subsequent SessionEnd calls with the same near-full-disk condition, the loop repeats. Partial .gz files accumulate at .1.gz, .2.gz, etc. The original .jsonl remains at >100 MB and is never pruned (prune only deletes files older than RETAIN_DAYS, not today's file).

The ENOSPC handler in log_tool_call.py silently drops new entries when disk fills — correct behavior, but by that point the disk may already be affecting other processes. There is no alerting or proactive size cap on the accumulating log.

findings.title: Stop hook transmits unredacted Claude response including any echoed secrets to the fast model API
evidence: The Stop hook is type 'prompt'. Claude Code sends the assistant's full response text to the configured fast model with the hook prompt prepended. This is a Claude Code runtime operation — not a hooks/lib operation.
redact.py is invoked only in the JSONL logging path (log_tool_call.py). It is never invoked on the response text before the Stop hook fires.

Scenario: user asks Claude to debug a database connection and shares their real connection URL (postgresql://user:PASS@host/db). Claude echoes the URL in its response. Stop hook ships the full response to Haiku. The URL-embedded password bypass (ADV-001) means redaction would not catch this even if it ran.

For a single-developer local setup this is low severity (primary and fast model share the same account). It becomes higher severity if the fast model endpoint differs in trust level, is a shared deployment, or enables response logging on the provider side.
This represents an implicit trust assumption: the Stop hook treats the fast model as equally trusted with the primary model for all response content.

residual_risks: The call_id-based join documented in LOGGING.md is structurally broken (ADV-005). Any downstream analytics tooling that correlates pre/post rows by call_id will silently produce empty joins, not errors.

The settings.json hooks merge overwrites existing user hook lists (ADV-003). A user who installs, adds custom hooks to ~/.claude/settings.json, then re-runs with --force will lose those hooks with no warning.
Database URL passwords and compound env-var passwords (ADV-001) persist in JSONL logs at full fidelity for up to 365 days. The redaction gap for these common patterns is systematic, not edge-case.

safety-block.sh quote-strip preprocessing (ADV-002) is an acknowledged approximation, but the approximation is exploitable for any pattern the hook owns exclusively that is not also covered by settings.json permissions.deny.
testing_gaps: test-redaction.sh has no cases for compound env-var names (DB_PASSWORD, APP_SECRET_KEY) or URL-embedded passwords. All current tests use isolated keyword=value patterns that do not exercise the word-boundary failure mode.
test-hooks.sh has no test for the bash -c 'quoted-dangerous-cmd' bypass of safety-block.sh.
No test validates that the call_id in a pre log row equals the call_id in the corresponding post log row. test-4 in test-hooks.sh checks duration_ms >= 100 but does not verify call_id consistency.
No concurrent-write test exercises the pair_path collision path under two simultaneous identical-input tool calls in one session.
